summary: Defines managed objects for IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/second baseband repeaters, often called hubs, so they can be monitored and managed over a network with SNMP. It was replaced by RFC 2108.

eli5.summary: A hub copies whatever it hears out to every plug. This memo gives a way to ask a hub how it is doing without visiting it.

questions: how to manage ethernet hubs with snmp
what traps does the repeater mib define
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let you monitor and manage an Ethernet repeater, or hub, from across the network.

tldr.problem: Operators needed a standard way to monitor and control IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/s baseband repeaters, often called hubs, without visiting each device.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a Repeater MIB of SNMP managed objects in three groups (basic, monitor and address tracking), organized by repeater, port group and port, plus three traps.
tldr.outcome: It updated RFC 1368 with clarifications and was replaced by RFC 2108.

facts.label: Trap throttle
facts.value: At least 5 seconds between traps of a type

today: RFC 1516 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 2108. It obsoleted RFC 1368 and was a Draft Standard.

sections.title: Scope and the Management Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 10 Mb/second baseband repeaters, sometimes called hubs. It sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212) for describing and naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) for core objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) for network access to the objects.

The objects represent attributes of a repeater as defined in Section 9 of the IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD standard. They may also be used to manage non-standard repeater-like devices, but objects for implementation-specific properties of such devices are out of scope. The definitions follow the IEEE draft P802.3K, and the counters are defined to match the IEEE ones so that one set of instrumentation can serve both the IEEE and IETF management standards.

The authors call this a Repeater MIB rather than a Hub MIB, because the word hub is also used for modular chassis that mix repeaters with token ring, FDDI, bridges and routers.
sections.eli5: There is already a rule book for how to ask machines questions. This memo adds the list of questions for one kind of machine, the Ethernet hub.

sections.title: Repeaters, Ports, Groups and MAUs
sections.content:
A repeater joins Ethernet-like segments so the network can be longer than one coax segment allows. Data that arrives on any port is sent out on each of the other n-1 ports, and if it arrives on two or more ports at once, or a collision is detected, the repeater sends a jamming signal out on all ports. All stations on its segments share a single collision domain. It is a bit-wise store-and-forward device, unlike a bridge, which handles whole frames. It is not an end-station, has no MAC address, and cannot be addressed by packets.

A repeater connects through Medium Attachment Units (MAUs), such as 10BASE-5, 10BASE-2, 10BASE-T and FOIRL. This MIB covers the repeater unit only. MAU management is left to a separate memo.

Because repeaters are often modular, ports are split into groups, for example one per card. A port is identified by group number and port number. rptrGroupCapacity and rptrGroupPortCapacity each have a maximum value of 1024. Groups and ports may come and go without a management reset and may be sparsely numbered. Internal ports, such as management ports, may be managed or not, and the capacity counts only managed ports.
sections.eli5: A hub is like a speakerphone for a room full of cables: whatever one says, everyone else hears. Cards and plugs are numbered, like 'card 3, plug 11', so you can ask about a specific one.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module is SNMP-REPEATER-MIB, rooted at snmpDot3RptrMgt, which is { mib-2 22 }. It has three groups. The Basic group is mandatory for all managed repeaters. The Monitor and Address Tracking groups are optional. Each group is split into subtrees for the repeater as a whole, for port groups, and for individual ports. In the address tracking package the repeater and group subtrees are currently unused.

The MIB relies on the MIB-II system group, which applies even if the entity only manages a repeater. The MIB-II interfaces group does not apply to repeater ports. A repeater port has no relation to a MIB-II interface, so that group covers only the network interfaces the managing entity uses for management traffic.

The only textual convention used is MacAddress, a 6-octet string. It does not change encoding or meaning and is for readers' convenience.
sections.eli5: The questions are sorted into three drawers. The first drawer must be in every hub. The other two are extras that a hub may include.

sections.title: What the Groups Contain
sections.content:
The Basic group holds status, parameter and control objects. At the repeater level these include rptrOperStatus (one of other, ok, rptrFailure, groupFailure, portFailure or generalFailure, reporting the highest priority failure), rptrHealthText, rptrReset, rptrNonDisruptTest and rptrTotalPartitionedPorts. There is a table of groups and a table of ports. Setting rptrPortAdminStatus to disabled(2) stops a port from transmitting or receiving until it is explicitly enabled again, and the port keeps that setting across power loss or reset.

Setting rptrReset to reset(2) makes the repeater go to the START state of the IEEE standard and run a disruptive self-test, after which the agent updates health information and sends an rptrHealth trap. The agent may delay the reset briefly so the SNMP response can be sent. rptrNonDisruptTest runs a non-disruptive self-test, and the definition allows an 'okay' result after only a trivial test.

The Monitor group has statistics for the repeater and each port, such as readable frames and octets, FCS errors, alignment errors, runts, collisions and auto-partitions. The Address Tracking group follows the MAC addresses of stations attached to each port. Counters are defined in terms of seven functions and signals from the IEEE draft, such as CollisionEvent, CarrierEvent, FramingError and FCSError, which are concepts used in definitions rather than retrievable objects.
sections.eli5: The first drawer says 'am I healthy?' and has buttons for 'restart' and 'turn this plug off'. The second counts how much traffic and how many mistakes each plug saw. The third remembers who was last plugged in where.

sections.title: Traps
sections.content:
Three SNMP traps, defined with the RFC 1215 conventions, let a repeater report events without being asked.

  • rptrHealth is sent when rptrOperStatus changes or when a non-disruptive test completes.
  • rptrGroupChange is sent when a group is logically or physically added to or removed from the repeater.
  • rptrResetEvent is sent on completion of a repeater reset triggered by a management command, but not when the agent restarts and sends a coldStart or warmStart trap.

The agent must throttle each trap type so there is at least a five-second gap between traps of that type. Throttled traps are dropped, not queued for later.
sections.eli5: Instead of waiting to be asked, the hub can ring a bell when its health changes, a card is added or removed, or it restarts. It will not ring the same bell more than once every five seconds.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1368
sections.content:
The update is a set of clarifications plus one deprecation. It adds the section on internal ports and MAUs, notes that the failure list for rptrOperStatus is ordered highest priority first, and clarifies rptrReset and rptrNonDisruptTest, including that the agent may briefly delay the action. It also deprecates rptrAddrTrackLastSourceAddress in favor of a replacement object (rptrAddrTrackNewLastSrcAddress) that has a zero-length value until the first frame is seen on the port. It clarifies that the rptrHealth trap is sent after rptrNonDisruptTest even if health information does not change, and clarifies the text on throttling traps.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: This version fixes confusing wording in the old one and swaps one question for a better-behaved version.
